Abstract This study explores how corporate social responsibility (CSR) commitment, top management support (TMS), and financial innovation (FI) influence sustainability performance (SP) through green finance (GF), highlighting GF as the operational bridge connecting organizational intent with sustainability outcomes. Using a cross-sectional quantitative design, data were collected from 632 professionals across finance, energy/renewables, manufacturing, and agriculture sectors between January and April 2025. Respondents included sustainability managers (28%), top executives (22%), innovation officers (19%), and CFOs (18%). Structural equation modeling (SmartPLS 4) was applied to validate the measurement model and test direct and mediating effects. The results show that financial innovation significantly enhances green finance (β = 0.466, p < 0.01) and that top management support also exerts a positive effect on green finance (β = 0.311, p < 0.01). Green finance, in turn, positively influences sustainability performance (β = 0.346, p < 0.01). However, the direct impact of CSR on green finance is negative and insignificant (β = −0.092, p > 0.05), suggesting that CSR alone does not automatically translate into green financial practices without enabling mechanisms. Mediation analysis further confirms that green finance channels the effects of financial innovation (β = 0.161, p < 0.01) and top management support (β = 0.107, p < 0.01) toward sustainability performance, while the CSR pathway remains unsupported (β = −0.032, p > 0.05). These findings emphasize role of green finance in operationalizing leadership commitment and financial innovation for sustainability outcomes. Policymakers need to strengthen green finance infrastructure, and firms need to integrate CSR initiatives with innovative financial instruments and executive support to achieve measurable environmental and social impact. Keywords: sustainable finance mechanisms, executive leadership engagement, eco-innovation strategies, environmental performance metrics, digital financial solutions 1. Introduction 1.1. Background and research context The increasing global focus on sustainable development has revolutionized the organizational value-creation strategy to a great degree, calling for companies to balance financial goals with green and social agendas. As climate change accelerates, natural resource depletion and social disparities intensify, and stakeholders such as regulators, investors, and customers demand more sustainable business practices and transparency in sustainability reporting (Robertson et al., 2022; Tolossa & Gota, 2023). In line with this, notions of corporate social responsibility (CSR), green finance, and financial innovation have been at the forefront of modern management, providing opportunities for companies to align profitability and sustainability (Jose et al., 2024; Adeyemi et al., 2024). Although the literature increasingly highlights the potential of CSR, top management support, and financial innovation in driving sustainability performance, the mechanisms through which these variables interact remain insufficiently understood (Abbas & Shahid, 2024; Kamran et al., 2022; Sheraz et al., 2025). This research aims to explore the direct and indirect relationships among CSR commitment, top management support, financial innovation, green finance, and sustainability performance. In particular, green finance is a mediator of the effects of CSR, financial innovation, and top management support on sustainability results. We conceptualize the study’s core constructs as follows: Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) refers to a firm’s strategic commitments and practices aimed at meeting stakeholder expectations and societal norms regarding environmental and social stewardship. Top Management Support (TMS) denotes senior executives’ sustained attention, resource allocation, and Multidiscip. Rev. Financial Innovation (FI) captures the development or adoption of novel financial instruments, processes, and analytics that reconfigure funding and risk-sharing to enable sustainability investments. Green Finance (GF) encompasses financial products, policies, and allocation decisions that channel capital specifically toward environmentally beneficial projects and activities. Sustainability Performance (SP) reflects measurable improvements in environmental outcomes (and related organizational KPIs) attributable to green investments and practices. Accordingly, we address the following research questions: To what extent do CSR commitment, top management support, and financial innovation influence the adoption of green finance? What is the impact of green finance on organizational sustainability performance? Does green finance mediate the relationships between CSR, financial innovation, top management support, and sustainability performance? The results of this research are important for both theoretical and practical purposes. For scholars, this study adds to the nascent literature on sustainability management by elucidating the mechanisms through which CSR, innovation, leadership, and sustainable value creation are connected (Ali et al., 2023; Dhir et al., 2023). For policymakers and practitioners, the results provide pragmatic recommendations on how to formulate and execute successful sustainability strategies, i.e., through the incorporation of green finance as an operational bridge (Tan et al., 2025; Sule et al., 2024). By sampling across industries via a heterogeneous sample, the study offers generalizable findings that can be used to inform sustainability efforts in diverse organizational settings. A number of theories inform this research in an integrated way. Stakeholder theory explains why firms face sustained pressures to align conduct with social and environmental expectations, making CSR commitment and top management support (TMS) strategically salient responses that shape priorities and accountability (Yang & Wang, 2019; McWilliams, 2020). Schumpeterian innovation theory clarifies how financial innovation (FI) reallocates capital toward novel, higher-productivity uses, creating new instruments and intermediation channels that can be oriented to sustainability investments (Smorodinskaya et al., 2019). Complementing this, institutional perspectives emphasize internal legitimation and rule structures through which executives embed sustainability logics in resource allocation, while the resource-based view (RBV) highlights the firm capabilities needed to design, evaluate, and deploy such instruments effectively. Taken together, these lenses imply that green finance (GF) functions as the operational bridge that translates CSR/TMS intentions and FI potential into observable sustainability performance (SP). Accordingly, we expect CSR, TMS, and FI to promote the adoption of GF (H1–H4) and, crucially, that GF mediates their effects on SP (H5–H7). 1.2. Conceptual framework Building on the construct definitions provided in the Introduction, we articulate how CSR commitment, top management support (TMS), and financial innovation (FI) jointly activate green finance (GF) to enhance sustainability performance (SP). CSR commitment shapes stakeholder expectations, internal identification, and organizational legitimacy—effects that can bolster employee motivation and performance and build trust with external stakeholders (Sagheer et al., 2022; Opondo & Nderitu, 2024). However, CSR’s influence often operates through pressure and orientation rather than direct capital allocation. Without instrumental enablers that translate intent into financing choices, CSR may remain symbolic, yielding uneven conversion into GF. FI lowers frictions and creates financing pathways by introducing instruments, processes, and analytics that reduce information and transaction costs, thereby improving financial intermediation, access, and risk sharing (Hernandez et al., 2018). Digitally driven innovations (e.g., fintech, blockchain) expand reach and liquidity, while also raising governance and systemic- risk considerations that require adaptive oversight (Chung et al., 2023; Agosto, 2021). Mechanistically, FI enables credible screening/monitoring, tailored pricing, and performance-linked structures that make green projects financeable. TMS coordinates attention, resources, and pace. Beyond formal authority, TMS provides sponsorship, resource allocation, and structural alignment for sustainability-oriented investments (Fareed et al., 2023). Its behavioral (e.g., funding, championing) and attitudinal (e.g., strategic commitment) dimensions accelerate implementation and reduce cancellation risks for high-investment, innovation-intensive initiatives (Vorwerk-Handing, 2012; Martinsuo & Anttila, 2022). In mechanism terms, TMS sets priorities and risk tolerance, catalyzing adoption of FI-enabled GF solutions. GF, as the operational bridge, channels capital toward environmentally beneficial projects via green bonds, sustainability-linked loans, ESG-screened portfolios, and policy-aligned instruments (Begum & Choudhury, 2024; Fareniuk, 2024). Effective GF regimes hinge on standards and transparency that reduce uncertainty and crowd in investors (Radhakrishnan, 2025). SP reflects measurable environmental improvements and related organizational KPIs over time, supported by performance management systems that integrate evidence-based targets and complement triple-bottom-line ambitions (Haque & Ntim, 2022; Nogueira et al., 2024). While short-term financial metrics may be mixed, sustained GF deployment generally strengthens compliance readiness, stakeholder trust, and strategic resilience. https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/mr Mocharref et al. Direct relations justification In stakeholder theory, corporate social responsibility reflects the sensitivity of a company to the environmental and social issues of its stakeholders. Green finance is positively affected by firms focusing on CSR since such firms invest money in green projects (Jose et al., 2024). Additional studies validate green investment initiatives as a CSR extension, aiding companies in achieving improved financial performance alongside environmental goals (Saher et al., 2023). H1. CSR commitment has a positive effect on green finance. Financial innovation is considered a facilitator of green finance, as it can increase the efficiency, accessibility, and diversity of sustainable financial instruments (Adeyemi et al., 2024). Financial innovation, as per Schumpeterian innovation theory, by redirecting capital to more productive and sustainable applications (Smorodinskaya et al., 2019). In green finance, emerging financial products such as green bonds, green leasing, digital finance, and carbon trading platforms reduce information asymmetries, enhance risk-sharing and draw in environmentally aware investors (Addy et al., 2024). showing that financial innovations such as digital finance and fintech products directly foster green innovation by easing financial constraints and enabling investment in green projects (Tang et al., 2023). Additionally, financial leasing has also been found to facilitate the transition toward green technology through providing flexible financing that enhances ecoefficient transitions (Hu & Wang, 2022). H2. Financial innovation positively influences green finance. Green finance has been established as a driver of sustainability performance in economic, environmental, and social aspects (Tan et al., 2025; Tolossa & Gota, 2023). In line with stakeholder theory, firms integrate the interests of wider stakeholder groups, such as communities, regulators, and the environment, into their financial decision-making (Robertson et al., 2022). that green financial practices have a positive influence on corporate sustainability performance (Abbas & Shahid, 2024; Jose et al., 2024; Tan et al., 2025). Moreover, a meta-analysis revealed that green finance is consistently associated with improved environmental performance through investment in pollution control and energy conservation technologies (Xu et al., 2020). H3. Green finance has a positive effect on sustainability performance. Top management support plays a role in advancing green finance initiatives within organizations by ensuring strategic alignment, dedicated resource allocation, and the internalization of sustainability as a core organizational value (Acharya et al., 2024). Drawing on institutional theory, organizational behaviors such as green financing are shaped not only by external pressures but also by internal legitimization processes led by executive leadership (Tian & Wang, 2024). When top executives demonstrate visible commitment to sustainability, it signals strategic prioritization, thereby fostering the integration of environmental considerations into financial planning and investment decisions (Kapoor et al., 2024). In this regard, empirical evidence confirms that strong leadership engagement is correlated with greater adoption of green financial instruments, highlighting the role of leadership in overcoming institutional inertia (Salma, 2024). H4. Top management support has a positive effect on green finance. 1.3.2. Indirect relation justification Green finance is a mediating channel whereby CSR practices are translated into improved sustainability performance (Wang et al., 2022). According to stakeholder theory, companies that are sensitive to stakeholder pressures for social and environmental accountability financial channels to achieve their sustainability goals (Yang & Wang, 2019). Whereas CSR commitment denotes the strategic intention of an organization to achieve environmental and social goals, the actual achievement of the same relies heavily on access to green financial products (Ali et al., 2023; Cai & Song, 2024; Kamran et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2022). H5. Green finance mediates the influence of CSR commitment on sustainability performance. Green finance can be considered a mediating mechanism through which the effect of financial innovation is transmitted to improve sustainability performance. Financial innovation, as an intangible resource based on resource-based view (RBV) theory, utilize green financial instruments that are the drivers of sustainable value creation (Sheraz et al., 2025). Financial innovations, for instance, fintech platforms or new investment instruments, lack direct environmental effects unless they are associated with sustainability objectives via green finance instruments (Addy et al., 2024; Hasan et al., 2024; Yang, 2024). Empirical evidence attests that green finance facilitates the conversion of innovation into environmental and social gains by leveraging capital flows into green projects, renewable energy, and low-carbon technologies (Hanson et al., 2024; Sule et al., 2024; Yang, 2024). Upper echelons theory explains that the strategic orientation and commitment of top managers influence organizational choice in the allocation of resources toward sustainability practices (Dhir et al., 2023; Mehjabeen, 2023). However, the realization of this strategic intention into tangible sustainability outcomes requires financial channels that clearly target green investments (Onipede, 2024). From this perspective, green finance can be considered an intermediary because it transforms executive-driven sustainability agendas into actionable projects, such as renewable energy investments and low-carbon technology (Sule et al., 2024). H7. Green finance mediates the relationship between top management support and sustainability performance. 2. Research Methodology 2.1. Research design In accordance with the conceptual framework outlined in Figure 1, the current study investigates the impact of corporate social responsibility (CSR) commitment and top management support on sustainability performance via financial innovation (Addy et al., 2024; Adeyemi et al., 2024) and green finance (Tan et al., 2025; Tolossa & Gota, 2023). In this context, green finance plays an intermediary role in guiding organizational effort in sustainable directions, and financial innovation facilitates the development of new financial instruments in favor of sustainability goals (Addy et al., 2024; Adeyemi et al., 2024; Hasan et al., 2024; Zhang, 2023). Figure 1 Research conceptual model. Methodologically, the study employs a cross-sectional quantitative research design to examine the hypothesized relationships. Data were collected at a single point to ascertain the views of finance and sustainability managers on how CSR, top management involvement, and financial innovation influence green finance and sustainability performance. Following a positivist paradigm, the current research focuses on empirically testing theory-based propositions via statistical inference (Chirkov & Anderson, 2018). Structural equation modeling (SEM) through SmartPLS 4 is applied to examine the complex relationships between the constructs (Sarstedt & Cheah, 2019). This is a method of tracing direct and mediating effects in the conceptual model to ensure consideration of the channels through which CSR participation and top management support influence sustainability performance through green finance and financial innovation. 2.2. Sample and data collection A structured questionnaire was the main data collection tool used in this research. Before large-scale data collection, pilot testing of a French version of the questionnaire was conducted, given the extensive use of the French language in the professional and academic community in Morocco. This pilot stage included a small group of financial managers and sustainability officers who reviewed the questionnaire for relevance, clarity, and cultural appropriateness. Their feedback was used to make necessary modifications, ensuring that the final questionnaire correctly measured the constructs being examined and was easily understandable to the respondents. The finalized questionnaire was circulated over four months, from January to April 2025. The target population comprised professionals in finance, sustainability management, and corporate governance to ensure that the respondents had adequate knowledge of CSR practices, financial innovation, and green finance initiatives. Using Slovin's formula, a sample size of 350 valid responses was determined to achieve statistical significance. Data gathering employed several channels, such as professional social networking websites, direct e-mail invitations, and in-person distribution during industry meetings and events. A total of 686 responses were gathered. After 54 invalid or incomplete entries were excluded, the resulting dataset included 632 valid responses, representing a large and diverse sample. https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/mr Mocharref et al. (2026) 5 The participants came from a wide range of industries, including finance and banking, manufacturing, textiles, and automotives. While industry-specific differences exist, these sectors share common issues related to sustainability performance and financial innovation. Analyzing the combined data enables the identification of generalizable insights into how CSR commitment and top management support influence green finance initiatives and ultimately drive sustainability outcomes across industries. 2.3. Measurement instruments To empirically test the proposed hypotheses, this study employed validated measurement instruments drawn from established frameworks in prior literature to ensure consistency and construct validity. Corporate social responsibility (CSR) commitment was assessed via a multi-item scale that captures a firm's strategic orientation toward environmental and social objectives (Jose et al., 2024). Top management support was measured through items reflecting executive involvement, leadership commitment, and resource allocation toward sustainability-driven initiatives (Acharya et al., 2024). Financial innovation was evaluated via perceptual indicators that reflect the creation and adoption of novel financial instruments, digital financial services, and sustainability-oriented investment solutions (Adeyemi et al., 2024). Green finance was operationalized through measures capturing the adoption of environmentally conscious financial instruments, investments in socially responsible projects, and the integration of environmental factors into financial strategies (Tan et al., 2025). Finally, sustainability performance was gauged via a comprehensive set of indicators spanning environmental, social, and governance (ESG) dimensions, which is consistent with methodologies commonly applied in the literature (Tolossa & Gota, 2023). 3. Direct relationship analysis Table 4 recapitulates the direct influences covered in the conceptual model and indicates the statistical backing for each hypothesis. The findings have implications for the main drivers of sustainability performance (SP) and green finance (GF). H1, which examines the impact of corporate social responsibility (CSR) on green financing, is not validated. The pathway coefficient is negative and statistically insignificant (β = –0.092, p > 0.05), indicating that CSR commitment does not directly result in green finance activities in the context being examined. This could be because CSR activities are not very compatible with green financial schemes or because their impact is provided through other channels. Conversely, H2 validates the existence of a positive and significant relationship between financial innovation (FI) and green finance (β = 0.466, p < 0.01), implying that innovative financial activities play a crucial role in enhancing the adoption of green finance. The results indicate that financial innovation is a major driver of the achievement of environmental integration into financial processes. H3 is also supported, as green finance has a positive effect on sustainability performance (β = 0.346, p < 0.01). This indicates the importance of green finance practices in improving firms' sustainability performance, possibly through environmentally friendly investment and resource optimization. Finally, H4 indicates that top management support (TMS) has a significant and positive effect on green finance initiatives (β = 0.311, p < 0.01), reflecting the paramount role of leadership in the integration of environmental finance practices into strategic decision-making. Indirect relationship analysis Table 5 reports the findings of the mediation test to examine how corporate social responsibility (CSR), financial innovation (FI), and top management support (TMS) indirectly influence sustainability performance (SP) through the mediating effect of green finance (GF). H5 tests the indirect influence of CSR on SP through green finance. The standardized beta is negative and nonsignificant (β = –0.032, p > 0.05; T = 2.67), implying that the mediation effect lacks meaningful influence. This could mean that CSR activities may not necessarily result in better sustainability performance if they pass through the channel of green finance, possibly due to poor integration between CSR activities and green financial measures. However, H6 reveals that financial innovation has a significant and positive indirect effect on sustainability performance through green financing (β = 0.161, p < 0.01; T = 7.356). This finding supports the mediating effect of green finance in leveraging financial innovation for sustainable implications. The robustness and significance of this effect demonstrate the necessity for innovative financial instruments in realizing sustainability aspirations. Likewise, H7 provides evidence of the statistically significant and positive mediating effect of green finance between top management support and sustainability performance (β = 0.107, p < 0.01; T = 5.518). This finding indicates that leadership commitment not only facilitates green finance but also indirectly contributes to sustainability performance, supporting the strategic function of executive support for sustainability initiatives. Research Discussion and Limitations The theoretical contributions of the findings imply a call for reconsidering linear assumptions in sustainability models. The inefficacy of the CSR commitment to green finance defies the conventional notion of stakeholder theory (Jose et al., 2024; Song et al., 2023), as it indicates that CSR, although strategic, can be devoid of operational impact if internal enablers are https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/mr Mocharref et al. (2026) 8 absent. This aligns with previous reservations that CSR by itself, unless supplemented by finance or managerial initiatives, risks being symbolic (Cai & Song, 2024; Kamran et al., 2022). Conversely, the established impact of financial innovation on green finance speaks to Schumpeterian innovation theory's insistence on innovation as an entrepreneurial approach to enhancing access to green financial instruments (Addy et al., 2024; Zhang, 2023). The beneficial impact of green finance on sustainability performance entrenches stakeholder theory, as it verifies that aligning financial flows with environmental agendas produces concrete results (Jose et al., 2024; Tan et al., 2025). Finally, the strong impact of top management support validates institutional theory, as it illustrates that leadership backing is necessary to integrate green finance into principal practices (Kapoor et al., 2024; Zhang & Xu, 2024). The results of the mediation have important theoretical implications for how green finance instrumentalizes internal and strategic drivers of sustainability performance. First, the indirect effect of CSR on sustainability performance through green finance is not statistically significant, suggesting that CSR alone may not lead to sustainability outcomes via green finance unless it is supported by additional mechanisms or organizational capabilities. Second, the mediating effect of green finance on the relationship between financial innovation and sustainability performance is consistent with the resource-based view (RBV), which places financial innovation as a strategic ability whose environmental utility is actualized by green-directed application (Addy et al., 2024; Sule et al., 2024). Third, the mediation of top management support through green finance reinforces upper echelons theory, indicating that the leadership vision only realizes sustainability outcomes when it is grounded in actionable financial initiatives (Dhir et al., 2023; Zhang & Xu, 2024). The results provide policy suggestions to policymakers, financial institutions, and corporate planners who seek to improve sustainability performance. First, the beneficial intermediation between financial innovation and sustainability performance necessitates investment in green fintech and digital platforms for the successful mobilization of funds to sustainable projects (Addy et al., 2024). This implies that policymakers should promote innovation-supportive ecosystems that catalyze the creation of scalable green finance instruments. Second, the intermediation function of green finance in translating top management support into sustainability performance implies greater executive-level involvement in sustainable investment policies (Kapoor et al., 2024; Zhang & Xu, 2024). Business organizations need to develop leadership cultures in which sustainability is embedded within financial planning and risk management. Overall, green finance needs to be institutionalized not only as an investment tool but also as a strategic bridge that aligns CSR vision, innovation potential, and leadership commitment with environmental and social performance measurement. While the results offer meaningful insights into the role of green finance as a mediating mechanism, several limitations should be acknowledged. First, the lack of a significant direct effect from CSR to green finance suggests potential contextual or institutional barriers that were not captured in the model. Prior studies have emphasized that CSR may require stronger internal structures or regulatory frameworks to activate green financial behavior (Cai & Song, 2024; Song et al., 2023). This finding indicates that in contexts with less mature sustainability ecosystems, CSR may remain declarative rather than operational. Second, the cross-sectional design limits the ability to capture dynamic interactions over time. Financial innovation and green finance evolve rapidly, and longitudinal data may better reflect their impact on sustainability . Third, the study may be influenced by self-reporting bias, particularly with respect to CSR and leadership support, which are prone to social desirability effects (Kamran et al., 2022). Finally, sectoral variations have not been explored in depth, despite evidence that green finance effectiveness differs across industries with varying environmental impacts. Addressing these limitations would strengthen the robustness and generalizability of future research on sustainability-oriented financial strategies. 5. Conclusion This research contributes to the literature on the mechanisms by which CSR commitment, top management support, and financial innovation complement one another in influencing sustainability performance, specifically through the mediating effect of green finance. Supported by strong theoretical underpinnings, the findings affirm that financial innovation and top management support contribute positively to the take-up of green finance, which has a positive and significant effect on sustainability performance. Interestingly, the influence of direct CSR commitment to green finance was not substantiated in the present setting, echoing the multifaceted and contextual nature of the impact of CSR. The results of the mediation analysis confirm that green finance serves as a significant transmission mechanism through which financial innovation and top management support enhance sustainability performance. However, the mediating role of green finance between CSR and sustainability performance is not statistically supported, suggesting that CSR may require additional organizational or contextual enablers to translate into measurable sustainability outcomes. These findings imply that although CSR is central to forming sustainability intentions, the successful realization of such intentions depends on the availability of innovative financial products and strategic leadership support. From a practical point of view, the research emphasizes that firms need to incorporate CSR initiatives with actual green financial frameworks and build innovation-facilitating cultures on the basis of executive leadership. Policymakers can also enable environments conducive to both financial innovation and green finance institutionalization for more general sustainability agendas. Although this study offers novel insights, it is not without limitations. Causal inference is limited by the cross-sectional design, and generalizability may be undermined by context-specific contingencies inherent in the sample. Longitudinal designs https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/mr Mocharref et al. (2026) 9 and more granular sectoral studies are recommended for future research to more precisely capture the dynamic interactions among CSR, green finance, innovation, and sustainability performance. Overall, this study highlights the strategic importance of green finance as an operational bridge between organizational intent and sustainable impact. JSON: Name: green_finance_mediation_sem Title: Quantitative structural equation modeling of green finance mediation in translating CSR, financial innovation, and top management support into organizational sustainability performance Short Hypothesis: Green finance mediates the positive causal effects of financial innovation and top management support on organizational sustainability performance. Related Work: Existing work has explored links among CSR, top management support, financial innovation, green finance, and sustainability performance primarily via cross-sectional surveys and correlational models. Approaches differ in statistical technique (covariance-based SEM vs. PLS-SEM), unit of analysis (individual perceptions vs. firm-level indicators), and operationalization of constructs (self-reported scales, binary adoption flags, or financial instrument counts). Limitations across current methods include heavy reliance on self-reported, cross-sectional data that weakens causal claims; insufficient use of multi-source firm-level outcome measures; limited tests of measurement invariance or predictive validity; inconsistent treatment of mediation and alternative causal pathways; and sparse sectoral or longitudinal disaggregation. Comparative weaknesses include sensitivity of covariance-based SEM to nonnormal data and small samples, while PLS-SEM studies often omit rigorous out-of-sample prediction checks. Few studies systematically compare mediation versus direct-only specifications, or evaluate robustness to multicollinearity, common-method bias, and alternative mediators, leaving questions about the operational role of green finance unresolved. Abstract: This research addresses whether green finance functions as the operational mediator that converts organizational capabilities—specifically financial innovation and top management support—into measurable sustainability performance. We propose a quantitative approach using structural equation modeling to compare direct-effect and mediated-effect specifications and to evaluate measurement validity, predictive power, and robustness across sectors. The main contribution is a validated empirical pipeline that (1) measures constructs with established multi-item scales and firm-level outcome indicators, (2) quantifies mediation effect sizes and predictive relevance, and (3) contrasts alternative models (direct-only, alternative mediators, and longitudinal cross-lagged models) to test causal direction. Expected outcomes include precise estimates of mediation strength, model fit and predictive metrics, and identification of contexts where green finance is an effective operational bridge. Results will clarify whether and how investments in financial innovation and leadership commitment translate into improved environmental and ESG performance via green finance instruments. Experiments: Datasets: (A) Primary cross-sectional survey: n=632 responses (finance, energy, manufacturing, agriculture) with item-level measures for CSR, TMS, FI, GF, SP; (B) Firm-level panel: matched financial and ESG indicators for ~300 firms over 3 years (annual), including green instrument issuance, capex in green projects, and environmental KPIs; (C) Synthetic perturbation datasets for sensitivity analysis (varying measurement noise, common-method bias, missingness). Baselines: (1) Direct-effects SEM: CSR, FI, TMS -> SP (no mediator); (2) Full mediation PLS-SEM: CSR, FI, TMS -> GF -> SP (proposed model); (3) Alternative mediator model: replace GF with Organizational Capability; (4) Covariance-based SEM (CB-SEM) equivalent of Model 2. Evaluation metrics: indicator reliability (loadings), internal consistency (Cronbach's alpha, composite reliability), convergent validity (AVE), discriminant validity (HTMT), multicollinearity (VIF), structural metrics (path coefficients with bootstrap CI, t-values, p-values), explanatory power (R^2), effect size (f^2), predictive relevance (Stone-Geisser Q^2), global fit (SRMR for PLS, RMSEA/CFI/TLI for CB-SEM), out-of-sample prediction (PLSpredict RMSE), and mediation indirect-effect significance via bootstrap (5,000 samples). Experimental setup: estimate PLS-SEM in SmartPLS 4 with 5,000 bootstrap resamples; estimate CB-SEM in lavaan with robust ML and bootstrap; run PLSpredict with 10-fold cross-validation for predictive assessment; conduct multi-group analysis by sector and respondent role; perform ablation studies removing each antecedent (CSR, FI, TMS) in turn and comparing changes in R^2 and indirect effects; perform cross-lagged panel SEM on firm-level panel to test temporal precedence (lag-1 effects of FI/TMS on GF and GF on subsequent SP). Report model comparison statistics, bootstrapped indirect-effect sizes and 95% CIs, and out-of-sample RMSE differences across models. Risk Factors and Limitations: Technical failure modes: model misspecification in SEM can produce biased path estimates; mediation inference from cross-sectional data risks reverse causality. Data and measurement biases: self-reported survey items introduce common-method variance and social desirability bias; nonresponse and sample weighting issues may distort representativeness. Evaluation biases: PLS-SEM may overfit without proper cross-validation; CB-SEM assumptions (normality, large N per parameter) may be violated. Scalability and compute limits: bootstrap and cross-validation on large panel data increase runtime and memory; complex multi-group and longitudinal models require careful identification and may suffer convergence failure. Statistical limits: small effect sizes, multicollinearity among antecedents, and heteroskedastic residuals reduce power and interpretability. Generalization limits: findings from the sampled industries and national context may not transfer to other regulatory or financial ecosystems; temporal generalization is limited if relying on cross-sectional data. Data availability constraints: obtaining reliable firm-level green finance issuance and standardized ESG KPIs for longitudinal matching may be incomplete or inconsistent across firms and years.
